title: 'I don't want to die': RCMP officer describes opening fire during chaotic attempted arrest that left man dead
article: An RCMP officer who fatally shot a man at an Alberta rest stop says a superior officer repeatedly told her the person she was approaching could either be the intended target of another shooting - or a suspect.

Const. Jessica Brown and Cpl. Randy Stenger are in their second week of a manslaughter trial for the shooting of Clayton Crawford, who was shot 10 times when Brown and Stenger opened fire on his truck at a rest area near Whitecourt in 2018.
The officers claim they fired in self defence as Crawford put the vehicle in reverse while trying to flee.

"He could have driven out of there, there was a clear path," Brown testified Wednesday, her voice heavy with emotion. "There's no reason to go backwards except to try to kill us. I keep thinking, 'I don't want to die. I don't want to get killed by this car.'"

Crawford was killed July 3, 2018. Brown, 31, told jurors the day began with a call from a civilian RCMP member, who told her an off-duty officer had spotted a distinctive purple pickup that was a vehicle of interest in a shooting in nearby Valhalla Centre the previous day.

Investigators believed two assailants opened fire through the door of a house where Crawford was staying with his girlfriend, wounding his girlfriend. Crawford - who police believed owed a drug debt to one of the shooters - fled in a purple Dodge Dakota pickup with the words "plum crazy" on the tail.
"I recognized right away this was a call where I'd need some backup," Brown testified.
Brown and four other officers including Stenger headed west down Highway 43. They stopped first to check a rest stop by the local casino, but saw no sign of the purple truck.

A short time later, Brown received another call from the Grande Prairie civilian who alerted her to the truck sighting. Brown said she was told the driver of the truck was "involved in a shooting" the previous day, and that he could be arrested for discharging a firearm with intent. Brown said the civilian told her the charges might be upgraded to attempted murder.

At 12:05 p.m., Brown spoke directly with Cpl. Eldon Chillog , the officer who flagged the purple truck as a vehicle of interest. Chillog earlier testified the purple truck was not a suspect vehicle and that he simply wanted Crawford's side of the story so he could identify the people who shot his girlfriend.
Brown said that during the call, Chillog told her he didn't know who was in possession of the purple truck and that it could be the suspect or the shooting's intended target.
"I was surprised at first. At first the only information I had been given was that this was a suspect vehicle," Brown said.
"He confirmed three or four times it could be either the shooting suspect or the intended target."

The Mounties then headed further west, where they spotted the purple truck at the Chickadee Creek rest area. Two officers stayed on the highway ready to throw a spike strip in case the vehicle fled. Brown, Stenger and Const. Ian Paddick drove to the purple truck but couldn't tell if anyone was inside.
The three then approached the truck, with Brown in the lead with her carbine. They saw a man reclined in the driver's seat, asleep. Paddick knocked on the window.

"The male in the vehicle wakes up, sits up, and puts his hands in the air, and is looking right at us," Brown said. "He was probably like that for two seconds. Then his eyes widened a bit, and he looked like he had this moment of clarity, that we were the police. He immediately dove down between his legs."

Worried he was reaching for a weapon, all three officers began shouting commands. Paddick smashed the window with a baton and tried to hold Crawford in his seat. Brown or Paddick opened the driver's door, but failed to prevent Crawford from starting the vehicle.
When the truck backed toward the officers, "I heard Randy's first shot," Brown said. "That's when I raised my carbine and started to shoot."
The truck eventually came to a stop in a tree line on the other side of Highway 43. Several hours passed before a specialized RCMP team approached the vehicle and confirmed Crawford was dead.
The trial began Nov. 21 and is scheduled for three weeks.
